questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man in rural New Mexico presents in July with 2 days of high fever, chills and a very swollen, exquisitely tender lump in the right groin. His cat had been hunting prairie dogs and had fleas. Temperature is 39.9 C (103.8 F), and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Aspirate of the groin node shows small gram-negative rods that stain darker at both ends, like a safety pin.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Oral metronidazole
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly
Gentamicin or streptomycin
Supportive care alone
Atovaquone-proguanil

explain.html:
A zoonosis is an infection with a non-human vertebrate reservoir, and Yersinia pestis is the classic example: its reservoir is rodents (rats, squirrels, gerbils, field mice, prairie dogs), endemic in much of the world including the western US, and fleas carry it to humans when a sickening animal's fleas leave to bite a new host; handling infected animals also transmits it. The organism is a small gram-negative rod with bipolar, safety-pin staining and a capsule. Plague has three clinical forms: septicemic (fever, hypotension), bubonic (fever with very swollen lymph nodes in the axilla or groin, which can spread to multisystem illness) and pneumonic. Organisms can be seen in node aspirates or sputum on Giemsa, Gram or fluorescent stains and can be cultured.

All forms have high mortality without treatment, and therapy is streptomycin or gentamicin, with doxycycline or quinolones as alternatives. This New Mexico man has a tender groin bubo, borderline blood pressure, a cat that hunted prairie dogs and carried fleas (the same risk as the 2024 Oregon pet cat case), and safety-pin rods in the aspirate, so he needs an aminoglycoside now.
explain.table:
Form of plagueFeatures
BubonicFever, very swollen axillary or groin nodes; may spread systemically
SepticemicFever, hypotension
PneumonicSevere bronchopneumonia; can spread through the air
All formsHigh mortality untreated; streptomycin or gentamicin
why: Metronidazole is not among the plague drugs (streptomycin, gentamicin, doxycycline, quinolones).
Penicillin treats early leptospirosis, not plague, which needs gentamicin or streptomycin.
All forms of plague have high mortality without treatment, so supportive care alone is wrong.
Atovaquone-proguanil is an antimalarial and has no role in a gram-negative zoonosis.
explain.takeaway: Yersinia pestis (rodent reservoir, flea vector, bipolar safety-pin gram-negative rod) causes bubonic plague, treated with streptomycin or gentamicin because untreated plague has high mortality.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 36-year-old musician who makes his own drums from imported goat hides notices a painless, itchy papule on his forearm. Over 5 days it becomes a painless ulcer with a black, depressed center surrounded by marked nonpitting edema. A Gram stain of the lesion shows large gram-positive rods with square ends, some with central spores.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: Local wound care only, since skin infection stays localized
Topical antibiotic ointment for 2 weeks
Surgical excision of the lesion without antibiotics
Antitoxin alone without antibiotics
Systemic ciprofloxacin, since the infection can disseminate

explain.html:
Bacillus anthracis is a large, aerobic, non-motile gram-positive rod with square ends and a central spore; the spores survive for years in soil. Anthrax is a disease of herbivores, and humans are infected by contact with infected animals or with spores in animal products, as in the Lehigh Valley drum maker who used African animal hides. The skin is the usual site of entry: the bacteria replicate and produce anthrax toxin, which causes edema, and a painless papule turns into an eschar. From the skin the bacteria can spread into lymphatics and cause severe illness and death.

Diagnosis is by culture of skin or blood, with PCR available. Because about 20% of cutaneous cases disseminate, cutaneous anthrax should always be treated with a systemic antibiotic, and ciprofloxacin is the treatment, with penicillin and doxycycline also used. This drum maker's painless black depressed ulcer with nonpitting edema and square-ended spore-forming rods is cutaneous anthrax.
explain.table:
Form of anthraxEntryPicture
CutaneousSkin (usual)Painless papule to eschar with edema; 20% disseminate
InhalationalAirborne sporesPneumonia, mediastinal hemorrhage, bacteremia, death
All formsCulture or PCRCiprofloxacin; penicillin or doxycycline also used
why: Cutaneous anthrax disseminates in about 20% of cases, so local care alone is never enough.
Topical therapy does not prevent spread through lymphatics.
Excision alone does not treat the infection, and a systemic antibiotic is always needed.
Antibiotics are the listed treatment, and antitoxin alone does not stop bacterial spread.
explain.takeaway: Cutaneous anthrax (painless eschar with edema after contact with animal hides) is always treated with a systemic antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin because about 20% disseminate.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old mail sorter develops fever, malaise and a dry cough, followed 3 days later by severe dyspnea, chest pain and hypotension. Chest radiograph shows a markedly widened mediastinum and a left lower lobe consolidation. Blood cultures grow large aerobic gram-positive rods that form spores.

Which of the following best explains his chest radiograph findings?
choices: Spirochetes reaching the lungs after exposure to rat urine
Bacteria seeding the lung from a flea bite in the axilla
Intracellular bacteria inhaled from dust around the placenta of a farm animal
Spores inhaled and germinating with toxin-driven mediastinal hemorrhage
Bird-derived intracellular bacteria causing interstitial pneumonia

explain.html:
Anthrax enters most often through the skin, but the respiratory tract is a less common portal. When Bacillus anthracis spores are inhaled, they germinate and the bacteria produce toxin, leading to pneumonia, mediastinal hemorrhage, bloodstream infection and death. The radiographic signature is a widened mediastinum, shown in the 2001 inhalational case with left lower lobe consolidation. That year anthrax was used in a bioterrorism event through the US mail, and anthrax remains the best known bioterrorism agent.

This mail sorter had a flu-like prodrome followed by severe dyspnea, chest pain and hypotension, a markedly widened mediastinum with left lower lobe consolidation, and large aerobic spore-forming gram-positive rods in the blood. The chest film reflects inhaled spores germinating with toxin-driven mediastinal hemorrhage.
explain.table:
ZoonosisHow the lungs are reachedOrganism
Inhalational anthraxInhaled spores; mediastinal hemorrhageGram-positive spore-forming rod
Pneumonic plagueSpread from bubo or airborneBipolar gram-negative rod
Q feverInhaled dust near birthing animalsCoxiella, intracellular
PsittacosisHandling birds or inhaled aerosolChlamydophila, obligate intracellular
LeptospirosisNot a pulmonary route; animal urine in waterSpirochete
why: Rat-urine spirochetes describe leptospirosis, which does not cause spore-forming gram-positive bacteremia or a wide mediastinum.
Flea-borne bipolar gram-negative rods describe plague, and they do not form spores.
Inhaling dust near a birthing animal describes Coxiella and Q fever, an intracellular organism, not a gram-positive rod.
Bird-derived intracellular bacteria cause psittacosis with interstitial pneumonia, not a widened mediastinum.
explain.takeaway: Inhalational anthrax follows inhaled Bacillus anthracis spores (classically bioterrorism) and causes pneumonia with toxin-driven mediastinal hemorrhage, seen as a widened mediastinum.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old woman who recently visited family in a village in Mexico has 6 weeks of fevers that come and go over days, night sweats, fatigue and low back pain. While there she ate fresh soft goat cheese made from unpasteurized milk. She has hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Blood cultures grow small gram-negative coccobacilli after prolonged incubation.

Which feature of this organism best explains her prolonged course?
choices: Production of a heat-stable toxin preformed in food
Survival within macrophages of the liver, spleen and marrow
Formation of spores that persist in soil for years
Invasion of red blood cells of all ages
Dormant hepatocyte forms that reactivate months later

explain.html:
Brucella species are small gram-negative coccobacilli that are primarily animal pathogens: B. melitensis from goats and sheep in Mexico and the Mediterranean causes more severe disease, B. abortus from cows and B. canis from dogs cause mild disease, and B. suis from pigs is severe. Infected animals shed the bacteria in milk for prolonged periods, and humans are infected through skin, alimentary tract or inhalation, with unpasteurized milk a recognized source and no human-to-human spread. From the portal of entry the bacteria go to lymph nodes and bloodstream and survive for prolonged periods in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes, producing a chronic granulomatous infection.

That persistence explains the clinical picture of gradual fever, malaise and sweats with an undulant (intermittent) fever, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis, and in some patients chronic waxing and waning symptoms. Acute disease is diagnosed by blood, marrow or node culture, and treatment is doxycycline, streptomycin or TMP-SMX. This woman's 6 weeks of on-and-off fever, sweats and hepatosplenomegaly after fresh goat cheese in Mexico fit B. melitensis.
why: A preformed heat-stable toxin causes rapid food poisoning, not weeks of undulant fever with organomegaly.
Spores that persist in soil for years describe Bacillus anthracis, not Brucella.
Invasion of red cells of all ages describes P. falciparum, not Brucella, which survives in macrophages.
Dormant liver forms that reactivate are a parasitic mechanism, not how Brucella persists.
explain.takeaway: Brucella (unpasteurized dairy, livestock) survives for long periods in the liver, spleen, marrow and nodes, causing undulant fever and chronic granulomatous infection.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man returns from a whitewater rafting trip in Costa Rica. A week later he develops fever, severe myalgias of the calves and headache that improve after several days. A few days after that he becomes jaundiced with reduced urine output and bleeding into the whites of both eyes.

[[labs 0]]

How was this infection most likely acquired?
choices: Handling a pet parrot
Bite of an Ixodes tick
Inhaling dust near a birthing animal
Water contaminated with animal urine
Eating undercooked ground beef

explain.html:
Leptospira interrogans is a spirochete that infects many domestic and wild animals, with dogs and rodents most important for human transmission. Infected animals shed large numbers of bacteria in urine, the bacteria survive in wet environments, and humans are infected through contaminated water or food entering a break in the skin or a mucous membrane or by ingestion, so farmers and water sports participants are at risk (rafting in Costa Rica is a cited setting). After 1 to 2 weeks the bacteria cause a flu-like febrile illness; most cases resolve, but some patients then develop hepatitis, jaundice, renal failure, aseptic meningitis and conjunctival or scleral hemorrhage, a biphasic illness.

The severe form, Weil disease, with hemorrhage and kidney and liver failure, occurs in 5 to 10% of patients. Diagnosis is by isolation from blood, CSF or urine, PCR, or a rise in agglutinating antibody, and penicillin or doxycycline works if started early. This rafter's fever and calf myalgias, followed after a lull by jaundice, oliguria, a creatinine of 4.1 and scleral bleeding, is Weil disease acquired from urine-contaminated water.
why: Handling a pet parrot transmits Chlamydophila psittaci, which causes atypical pneumonia, not biphasic jaundice and renal failure.
Ixodes ticks transmit Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and babesiosis, while Leptospira is shed in animal urine into water.
Inhaling dust near a birthing animal describes Q fever.
Undercooked ground beef carries E. coli O157:H7, while Leptospira is shed in animal urine into water.
explain.takeaway: Leptospira interrogans is acquired from water contaminated with animal urine through skin or mucosa and causes a biphasic illness that can progress to Weil disease (jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage).
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman who breeds parakeets and cockatiels in her home develops fever, severe headache and a dry cough. Two of her birds recently became lethargic and died. Chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Her spleen is palpable. Routine sputum culture grows only normal flora.

Which of the following is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: A fourfold rise in antibody titer between acute and convalescent sera
Gram stain of the sputum showing many gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci
Culture of the sputum on chocolate agar for 48 hours
Thin blood smear for intraerythrocytic organisms
Darkfield microscopy of the sputum for spirochetes

explain.html:
Chlamydophila psittaci is an obligate intracellular, coccoid organism that infects parrots and most other bird species and is present in the blood, tissues, feces and feathers of an infected bird. Humans are infected by handling birds or inhaling aerosolized bacteria, and person-to-person spread is very rare. The bacteria enter the respiratory tract and spread to the reticuloendothelial cells of the liver and spleen, then hematogenously; the usual result is an atypical, interstitial pneumonia that can be severe, sometimes with aseptic meningitis or sepsis.

Psittacosis is rarely diagnosed unless someone asks about the exposure, with fewer than 10 US cases a year. Diagnosis is serologic: a fourfold increase in titer by complement fixation between acute and convalescent sera, and treatment is doxycycline or a macrolide. This parakeet and cockatiel breeder, whose birds died, has fever, headache, dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates and a palpable spleen, so paired sera confirm it.
explain.table:
ZoonosisMain diagnostic approach
PsittacosisFourfold titer rise on acute and convalescent sera
TularemiaSerology; warn lab before culture
Q feverPCR early, Coxiella IgG later
Cat scratch diseaseSerology; cultures negative
PlagueStains of node aspirate or sputum; culture
Brucellosis (acute)Blood, marrow or node culture
why: Gram-positive diplococci point to a typical bacterial pneumonia, not an obligate intracellular organism.
An obligate intracellular organism does not grow on routine agar; chocolate agar culture is used for tularemia.
A thin smear for intraerythrocytic organisms looks for blood parasites, not Chlamydophila.
Darkfield looks for spirochetes, and C. psittaci is coccoid.
explain.takeaway: Chlamydophila psittaci from birds causes atypical pneumonia with liver and spleen spread, is diagnosed by a fourfold titer rise on paired sera, and is treated with doxycycline or a macrolide.

explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 10-year-old boy has a 3-week history of a tender, enlarged lymph node in his left axilla. His family adopted a kitten 6 weeks ago, and he had a small crusted papule on his left hand a few weeks before the node enlarged. He is otherwise well. Blood cultures are negative.

Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Culture of an aspirate from the lymph node
Peripheral blood smear for morulae
Serology for Francisella tularensis
Lymph node aspirate stained for bipolar rods
Serology for Bartonella henselae

explain.html:
Bartonella species are fastidious gram-negative coccobacilli, and three cause human illness. B. henselae lives in cats with a flea reservoir and causes cat scratch disease, a regional lymphadenopathy that may drain and can occasionally disseminate to liver, spleen or CNS. In immunocompromised patients the same species causes bacillary angiomatosis, bacteremia and endocarditis. Diagnosis depends on the syndrome: blood culture is used for endocarditis and may be positive in bacillary angiomatosis, but for cat scratch disease the test is serology, because organisms may be seen on tissue while cultures are not positive.

There is no real consensus on whether antibiotics change the course of cat scratch disease. This boy has a tender axillary node draining the hand where a papule appeared after his family adopted a kitten, and his blood cultures are negative, so Bartonella henselae serology confirms the diagnosis.
why: Bartonella cultures are not positive in cat scratch disease, so a node culture will not confirm it.
Morulae point to ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis, not Bartonella.
Tularemia can follow cat contact, but a regional node after a kitten scratch with a papule is the classic cat scratch picture.
Bipolar safety-pin rods in a node aspirate suggest plague, which causes a febrile, exquisitely tender bubo with high mortality.
explain.takeaway: Bartonella henselae from cats causes regional lymphadenopathy (cat scratch disease), diagnosed by serology because cultures are negative.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

rows.if_right: bacillary angiomatosis in an immunocompromised host, where skin and node tissue can be cultured

rows.why: Morulae point to ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis, not Bartonella.
rows.if_right: fever, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after a Lone Star or Ixodes tick bite

rows.why: Tularemia can follow cat contact, but a regional node after a kitten scratch with a papule is the classic cat scratch picture.

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man who has been living in a crowded shelter with body lice has recurrent bouts of fever lasting several days, with leg pain and headache. Blood cultures are positive for a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus from a genus that also causes cat scratch disease. Public health officials note that, unlike its relatives, this species has no animal reservoir.

Which of the following illnesses is this organism classically known for?
choices: Oroya fever followed by verruga peruana
Trench fever
Rickettsialpox
Relapsing fever from Borrelia
Epidemic typhus from Rickettsia

explain.html:
The three Bartonella species that cause human illness are separated by vector and reservoir. B. quintana is transmitted by lice and has no animal reservoir, which makes it the exception in a lecture about zoonoses; it causes trench fever, described in World War I, and bacillary angiomatosis, bacteremia and endocarditis in HIV and other immunocompromise. B. bacilliformis is restricted to the Andes of Peru, Ecuador and Colombia and spread by sandfly bites; it causes Oroya fever (fever with hemolytic anemia) followed by angioproliferative skin nodules called verruga peruana. B. henselae lives in cats with a flea reservoir and causes cat scratch disease and bacillary angiomatosis.

This man in a crowded shelter has body lice, recurrent fevers with leg pain and headache, and a Bartonella species with no animal reservoir in his blood. That is B. quintana, the organism of trench fever.
explain.table:
SpeciesVector or reservoirClassic illness
B. quintanaLice; no animal reservoirTrench fever; bacillary angiomatosis, endocarditis
B. bacilliformisSandflies, AndesOroya fever, then verruga peruana
B. henselaeCats and fleasCat scratch disease; bacillary angiomatosis
why: Oroya fever and verruga peruana come from sandfly-borne B. bacilliformis in the Andes, not louse-borne disease.
Rickettsialpox is caused by Rickettsia akari from rodent mites, not by a louse-borne Bartonella.
Relapsing fever is a Borrelia illness, a different genus from the Bartonella in the stem.
Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia, not Bartonella, even though lice are involved.
explain.takeaway: Bartonella quintana (body lice, no animal reservoir) causes trench fever, B. bacilliformis (sandflies, Andes) causes Oroya fever, and B. henselae (cats and fleas) causes cat scratch disease.

explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old field biologist who traps ground squirrels in the western US is hospitalized with fever, cough productive of bloody sputum and rapidly worsening hypoxemia. Sputum Giemsa stain shows small gram-negative coccobacilli with bipolar staining. Several days earlier she had a painful swollen axillary node.

Which of the following precautions is most important for staff caring for her?
choices: Contact precautions for draining wounds only
Avoiding shared food and water containers
Standard precautions only, since no human spread occurs
Respiratory isolation for airborne droplet spread
Protection from mosquito bites on the ward

explain.html:
Plague from Yersinia pestis reaches humans from rodents, usually through fleas or by handling infected animals, and it is usually not transmitted person to person. The exception is the pneumonic form, a severe bronchopneumonia that can spread through the air. Bubonic disease can progress to generalized spread and multisystem illness, including the lungs. For that reason plague prevention lists quarantine and isolation along with rodent control, chemoprophylaxis and vaccine.

This field biologist traps western ground squirrels, had a painful axillary bubo days ago, and now has bloody sputum, worsening hypoxemia and bipolar gram-negative coccobacilli on sputum Giemsa stain. That is pneumonic plague, so staff need respiratory isolation in addition to her treatment with streptomycin or gentamicin.
why: Wound precautions alone miss the airborne spread that the pneumonic form allows.
Plague is spread by fleas and handling infected animals, not by shared food or water.
Most plague is not spread between people, but pneumonic plague can spread through the air.
Fleas, not mosquitoes, transmit plague, and the ward risk is airborne spread.
explain.takeaway: Plague is usually not spread between humans, but pneumonic plague can spread through the air and requires respiratory isolation.

explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

rows.if_right: a food- or waterborne zoonosis such as leptospirosis from contaminated water

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old landscaper on an island off Massachusetts presents in August with 4 days of fever, chills, dry cough and pleuritic chest pain. He mows large commercial lawns and recently ran over a rabbit nest. Chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe infiltrate with hilar adenopathy. Routine sputum and blood cultures are negative at 48 hours.

Which of the following is the most appropriate step regarding laboratory testing?
choices: Request a Wright stain of blood for morulae
Report the blood cultures as final negatives at 48 hours
Send serology and warn the laboratory before any culture
Order a thin and thick smear of the blood
Request a darkfield exam of the sputum

explain.html:
Francisella tularensis is a very small, fastidious, strictly aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus and an intracellular pathogen that enters macrophages. Rabbits and hares (lagomorphs) carry the subspecies that cause human disease, and people are infected by contact with an infected animal's skin, by inhalation, or by a tick that has fed on one. Its forms follow the portal of entry: ulceroglandular, oculoglandular, glandular, typhoidal, oropharyngeal or GI, and pneumonic, which can be severe with sepsis; summer outbreaks of pneumonic tularemia struck landscapers on Martha's Vineyard, linked to commercial lawn mowers.

Diagnosis is usually by serology. Culture on chocolate agar or BCYE can be done, but the laboratory must be warned because handling the organism carries a high risk of infecting lab personnel, and blood cultures usually will not turn positive before day 5. This landscaper mowed over a rabbit nest and has pneumonia with hilar adenopathy and negative cultures at 48 hours, so the next step is serology with a warning to the lab; treatment is streptomycin or gentamicin.
why: Morulae on a Wright stain point to ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis, not tularemia.
Tularemia blood cultures usually will not turn positive before day 5, so 48 hours is far too early to call them final.
Thick and thin smears look for blood parasites, not a gram-negative coccobacillus.
Darkfield microscopy looks for spirochetes, and F. tularensis is a coccobacillus.
explain.takeaway: Tularemia (rabbits, lawn mowing over nests, ticks) is diagnosed mainly by serology, and the lab must be warned before culture because F. tularensis readily infects lab staff.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

rows.if_right: fever, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after a Lone Star or Ixodes tick bite

questions.stem:
Four men develop fever, severe headache and dry cough about 2 weeks after a weekly card game held in a garage where a cat had given birth to kittens. Chest radiographs show bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Aminotransferases are mildly elevated, and a liver biopsy in one man shows granulomas. Routine bacterial cultures are negative.

Which long-term complication is this organism known for?
choices: Megacolon
Nephrotic syndrome
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Tabes dorsalis with locomotor ataxia
Culture-negative endocarditis

explain.html:
Coxiella burnetii is an intracellular rickettsial organism that resists desiccation, heat and sunlight and persists in soil with an endospore-like form; it is not cultured by usual methods, which is how Q (query) fever got its name. It infects many animals and is most concentrated in the placenta, so it can be present wherever an infected animal gives birth, and the usual route is inhalation of aerosolized soil near a pregnant animal (or ingestion of unpasteurized milk or cheese). Acute infection is usually an atypical pneumonia with bilateral infiltrates, fever and headache, and hepatitis is common, usually granulomatous.

Acute illness may resolve spontaneously, but some cases become chronic, causing culture-negative endocarditis or osteomyelitis. Diagnosis is PCR early and Coxiella IgG serology after a week; acute disease gets a tetracycline and chronic disease combination therapy. These four men fell ill after a card game in a garage where a cat had given birth, the same poker cluster the lecture cites.
explain.table:
ZoonosisChronic or late complication in this lecture
Q feverCulture-negative endocarditis, osteomyelitis
BrucellosisChronic infection with fatigue and intermittent fever; endocarditis rare
BartonellaEndocarditis; bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromise
LeptospirosisWeil disease: hemorrhage, kidney and liver failure
why: Megacolon is a late complication of Chagas disease, not of Q fever.
Nephrotic syndrome is a complication of P. malariae malaria, not of Q fever.
Hemolytic uremic syndrome is not a Coxiella complication.
Tabes dorsalis is late neurosyphilis, not a Q fever complication.
explain.takeaway: Coxiella burnetii (inhaled where animals give birth) causes atypical pneumonia with granulomatous hepatitis, and chronic Q fever causes culture-negative endocarditis.

explain.objective: Understand the microbiology and clinical features of multisystem bacterial zoonotic infections

questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 2 years ago and takes tacrolimus and prednisone develops several red-purple, raised, vascular-appearing skin nodules on his arms and trunk, plus fever. Imaging shows multiple blood-filled cystic spaces in the liver. He has two cats at home and has had flea bites. Biopsy of a skin nodule shows proliferating small blood vessels with clumps of bacilli on silver stain.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Benznidazole
Intravenous artesunate
Doxycycline or a macrolide
No antibiotics; the illness is self-limited
Metronidazole

explain.html:
Bacillary angiomatosis is the form of Bartonella infection seen in immunocompromised patients: vascular proliferative nodules in the skin that can also occur in the liver as peliosis hepatis or in the spleen. It is caused by B. henselae, the cat and flea species, and B. quintana causes it as well in HIV and other immunocompromise; a solid organ transplant patient is a pictured example. Blood culture may be positive, and skin and lymph node specimens can be cultured. Biopsy shows proliferating small vessels with bacilli on silver stain.

Unlike cat scratch disease in a healthy host, where there is no consensus that antibiotics help, bacillary angiomatosis and Bartonella endocarditis are treated with doxycycline or a macrolide. This kidney recipient on tacrolimus and prednisone, with cats and flea bites, red-purple vascular nodules, fever and blood-filled liver cysts, has bacillary angiomatosis.
explain.table:
Bartonella syndromeHostDiagnosisAntibiotics
Cat scratch diseaseHealthySerology; cultures negativeNo consensus
Bacillary angiomatosisImmunocompromisedBlood, skin or node cultureDoxycycline or macrolide
EndocarditisEitherBlood cultureDoxycycline or macrolide
why: Benznidazole is an antiparasitic for Chagas disease, not a treatment for a gram-negative coccobacillus.
Intravenous artesunate treats severe malaria, not Bartonella.
Unlike cat scratch disease in a healthy host, bacillary angiomatosis is treated.
Metronidazole is not the listed treatment for any Bartonella syndrome.
explain.takeaway: Bacillary angiomatosis (vascular skin nodules, peliosis hepatis) in immunocompromised hosts is caused by Bartonella and treated with doxycycline or a macrolide.
